summary:
Afyonkarahisar stands entirely under Turkey's national legal and policing framework on LGBTI+ matters. The draft omnibus justice package reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 contains no Afyonkarahisar-specific provision, and no provincial record exists that would make this province either more protective or more hostile than the country-wide picture. A visitor to Afyonkarahisar is subject to the same national rules, the same document regime and the same street-level policing practice documented elsewhere in Turkey.

The leaked '11th Judicial Package' would open the way to criminal charges against LGBT people. Conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', including its so-called 'promotion', would carry up to three years in prison; participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies would carry up to four years, and because same-sex marriage is not legal in Turkey such ceremonies are by definition symbolic. Human Rights Watch called the draft one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades. The measure had not been enacted when reported, but authorities have already been documented acting against trans people as though comparable prohibitions were in force.

The same draft would restrict gender-affirming care: the minimum surgery age raised from 18 to 25, permanent infertility imposed as a condition, medical professionals fined or imprisoned for up to seven years, and transgender patients facing up to three years for care falling outside the new limits. Rights groups assess that these limits would push transition care into underground settings.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, 'A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy', records 313 violations of the right to liberty, roughly two and a half times the previous year's total and consisting mostly of detentions, alongside 336 violations of the right to assembly and 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51. The torture figure is linked mainly to peaceful assembly, and the report documents event-specific bans together with violent police attacks on peaceful gatherings. These are national figures; no Afyonkarahisar-specific finding appears in the source.

The same report records six right-to-life violations in 2025, three of them counted as hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. These totals are compiled from media and civil-society reporting because the Turkish state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so the true figure cannot be verified from official records.

Hostility has been institutionalised under a 'Year of the Family' banner: instructions issued to public institutions, hate speech from senior officials, censored broadcasts and cancelled artistic events. The source presents this as national practice rather than a choice available to any province, which means it applies in Afyonkarahisar as it does in Istanbul or Ankara.

Two national rules bear directly on a trans visitor's exposure at any checkpoint. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance, and police conducting 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) stops have required trans women to produce documents. Any such interaction is an occasion on which passport details can be compared against presentation. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for GBT checks before release; that city-level pattern is one illustration of a national practice, not a separate local regime.

Two further national measures shape what a trans person faces if detained. Trans prisoners are placed according to registered sex rather than gender identity, confirmed by the death of the transgender prisoner Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025 and by the parliamentary question filed by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option on gender-related medical-board reports and required electronic reports, a change assessed as risking the profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch describes the draft package as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades, a framing that places the current Turkish position at the severe end of European practice rather than within ordinary regional variation.

The pattern has depth rather than being a single legislative moment. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, based on more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people; it predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's continuity, not as a statement of current law.

Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia. Istanbul Pride is the country's most visible single flashpoint and should be read as an indicator of national direction, not as a distinct local rule.

The asymmetry of state response is documented at case level. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Legal experts cited in reporting on GBT stops argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which Turkey has ratified. The argument concerns the legality of the stop itself, not only its outcome.
localsOnly:
Kaos GL compiles its violation counts from media and civil-society reports because the state maintains no official hate-crime statistics. Residents therefore have no official channel through which to establish the scale of anti-trans violence, and the association's annual totals are the working reference for advocacy.

The 'Year of the Family' designation operates as an instruction to public institutions, and the resulting hostility is expressed through hate speech from senior officials, censorship of broadcasts and cancellation of artistic events. For residents this reaches employment, public service delivery and cultural participation, not only policing.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

The Sincan Women's Prison case drew a coordinated response from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanding an independent investigation. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before Poyraz's death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken.

The Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 followed a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports. For residents already in the system, the change alters how transition care is recorded and authorised, and online framing of it as an 'LGBT opening' is contested.

Assembly is the most heavily policed site of LGBTI+ life: Kaos GL records 336 assembly violations in 2025, event-specific bans and violent police attacks on gatherings, with 89 torture or ill-treatment violations mostly linked to peaceful assembly.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Afyonkarahisar-specific reporting on LGBTI+ policing, local bylaws or provincial enforcement appears in the source inventory. Whether the province applies national practice more or less aggressively than Istanbul or Ankara is unresolved and not sourced here.

The '11th Judicial Package' was a leaked draft as of 29 October 2025. Whether it has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn is unresolved in this record; the penalties described are those of the draft, not of law in force.

Kaos GL's 2025 totals are compiled from media and civil-society reports rather than official statistics, and the state publishes no hate-crime data. The counts should be read as documented minimums, not as a complete measure of incidence.

The claim that GBT stops violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights is attributed to legal experts cited in reporting; no court ruling establishing that position is sourced here.

Whether the Health Ministry regulation of September 2025 has been challenged in court, and its precise effect on access to transition care in practice, is not sourced in this inventory.
